stages.name: Minimum prices
stages.title: Minimum prices
stages.sub: How a minimum price above equilibrium creates a surplus, and why that brings both benefits and problems.

steps.q: The government sets a legal minimum price for milk, above the price where the market would naturally settle. At this higher price, do farmers want to sell more milk or less than before?
steps.right: More, because the price is higher
steps.wrong: Less, because fewer people will buy it
steps.hint: Think about the supply curve: as price rises, what do producers want to do?

steps.q: At this minimum price, the quantity farmers want to supply is bigger than the quantity buyers want to demand. What exists in the market as a result?
steps.wrong: A shortage of milk for buyers
steps.hint: Supply exceeds demand at this price. What happens to the difference between them?

steps.q: Because farmers can sell all their milk at this guaranteed higher price rather than a lower market price, what happens to their earnings compared with before?
steps.right: They are protected and more stable
steps.wrong: They fall because less is sold overall
steps.hint: Think about what a price floor guarantees the seller, regardless of the surplus.

steps.right: Less, because it now costs more
steps.wrong: More, because it seems more valuable

steps.q: All that unsold surplus milk still has to go somewhere. Does keeping or getting rid of it cost anyone anything?
steps.right: Yes, someone has to pay to store or destroy it
steps.wrong: No, it disappears at no cost
steps.hint: Milk does not vanish. What has to happen to it, and who pays for that?

steps.q: Some buyers are unwilling to pay the high legal minimum price. Might they look for a way to get milk more cheaply, outside the legal market?
steps.right: Yes, an illegal cheaper market could appear
steps.wrong: No, they will always pay the legal price
steps.hint: If people want a cheaper deal and the legal price will not fall, where might they turn?
